Started a project in Svelte after spending about two afternoons trying to do it in React. Finds Svelte much simpler and more powerful than React, and criticizes React for handling only the UI layer while being too unopinionated about application architecture.

The breaking changes were rough this year, but the new SvelteKit structure is a big improvement. It is now very clear in what order items load and what loads on the server vs the client. Form actions are also amazing.

Finished a job using Svelte/SvelteKit, Tailwind, Postgres and TypeScript while new to the whole stack, and it went 'smooth as butter'. The breaking changes were a bit of a pain but not that bad. Main gripe: using folders to organize both layout hierarchy and route hierarchy is going to turn out to be a mistake.
After 1.5 years of using Svelte/SvelteKit full-time, says it is without comparison the most enjoyable and productive web framework they've ever used.

Complaint about the SvelteKit 1.0 launch: the site displayed 'This app requires modern web platform features. Please use a browser other than Safari.' The commenter concluded it looks cool but is not production ready.

Chose Svelte for the UI of a cross-platform video editing app with a Rust backend. Svelte Stores and the Context system are great for sharing state, and the app feels snappy. The generated code is readable: they stepped through compiled component code while profiling a layout-per-frame issue and traced it to their own function.
Mostly a back-end developer, found Svelte the most accessible frontend option: readable, good/simple docs with lots of examples, easy getting-started instructions, and a clear conceptual framework.

After ~5 years of React and some Vue, finds Svelte appealing for its fewer higher-level abstractions and for being 'less annoying'. Concedes React's larger ecosystem helps with big apps, and wishes SvelteKit were at Next.js's level, since fixing dev server errors is distracting.

Found the Svelte compiler easy to work with: importing it to prerender a component into an HTML string was trivial, and hooking into its preprocessing to add TypeScript via Deno's emit was simple. Says the documentation could be improved.
Has used Svelte for about a year and loves it, but the lack of community mindshare meant rolling a lot of their own components. Uses SvelteKit happily on Netlify.
Their team migrated a huge, complex React app to Svelte/SvelteKit in a month, and the difference was 'night and day' in performance, bundle size and dev productivity.
A Vue developer finds Svelte close to Vue's 'script setup' mode, but notes Svelte doesn't support JSX/TSX.

Experience with Svelte 4 on UIs with many elements: rendering usually causes performance problems before interactivity does, at about the same element count whether or not elements are interactive. The solution is to move to a canvas.
Praises Svelte 3's built-in compile-time accessibility warnings (e.g. 'A11y: element should have an alt attribute'), saying accessibility advocates have wanted this in mainstream tools for years.

A weak point for Svelte, as with Ractive before it, is the lack of a clear unit testing solution or docs, which weakens it in businesses' eyes. Better docs and samples in the quick start guides would help.
Tried to set a component's tag name dynamically with <svelte:component this={"h1"}>, as they do in React, but it doesn't accept strings, only Svelte components.
The interactive tutorial with sandboxes is really impressive and a great onramp, though it would be nice to be able to 'eject' a sandbox into a working local build.
Gave Svelte a chance around version 2, but it failed badly during a project because of Svelte transpiling bugs.
Dislikes Svelte's single-file component approach with custom template parsing. Argues JSX render functions are more composable and easier to test without framework-specific template compilers.

Loves Svelte's compile-to-imperative-JS idea, but because it's effectively a superset of JavaScript, IDE support has been an issue. They also struggled to find a solid UI component library, which has limited their Svelte use to smaller projects.
